title: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)
subject: gastroenterology
summary: Steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor with little or no alcohol. Stage fibrosis stepwise with FIB-4 then elastography, treat with weight loss (5% for fat, 7 to 10% for inflammation, 10% or more for fibrosis), manage cardiometabolic risk, and refer intermediate or high fibrosis risk to hepatology for MASH-targeted therapy.

sections.title: Definition
items: MASLD: hepatic steatosis (imaging or histology) plus at least 1 cardiometabolic criterion, with no other cause and alcohol below 140 g/week (women) or 210 g/week (men).
Cardiometabolic criteria (any one): BMI 25 or more (23 or more in Asians) or raised waist circumference; fasting glucose 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) or more, HbA1c 5.7% or more, or type 2 diabetes.
Or: BP 130/85 mmHg or more or treated; triglycerides 150 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L) or more or treated; HDL 40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L) or less in men or 50 mg/dL (1.3 mmol/L) or less in women, or treated.
MetALD: MASLD with alcohol 140 to 350 g/week (women) or 210 to 420 g/week (men). Above this, the disease is alcohol-related liver disease.

Highest risk of progressive fibrosis: type 2 diabetes, abdominal obesity, men over 50, postmenopausal women and multiple metabolic risk factors. Liver enzymes may be normal even with advanced fibrosis.

sections.title: Case-finding and fibrosis staging
items: Look for MASLD with fibrosis in type 2 diabetes, abdominal obesity with 1 or more other metabolic risk factor, abnormal liver tests, or incidental steatosis on imaging. Do not screen the general population.
Exclude other causes: alcohol history (quantity and pattern), HBsAg, anti-HCV, ferritin and transferrin saturation, steatogenic drugs, and autoimmune or metabolic liver disease when suggested.
Step 1: FIB-4. Below 1.3 (below 2.0 if over 65) = low risk: repeat in 1 to 2 years if diabetes or 2 or more risk factors, otherwise 2 to 3 years.

Step 2 (FIB-4 1.3 or more): vibration-controlled transient elastography (low risk below 8 kPa, intermediate 8 to 12 kPa, high above 12 kPa) or ELF test (low below 7.7, intermediate 7.7 to 9.8, high above 9.8).
Ultrasound is not needed to make the diagnosis and cannot stage fibrosis. Liver biopsy is reserved for indeterminate non-invasive tests or diagnostic uncertainty.

Assess comorbidities at diagnosis and follow-up: HbA1c, lipids, BP, renal function and urine albumin, sleep apnoea, and cardiovascular risk. Cardiovascular disease and non-liver cancers are the leading causes of death in MASLD without advanced fibrosis.

sections.title: Lifestyle (all patients)
items: Overweight or obesity: sustained weight loss of 5% or more reduces liver fat, 7 to 10% improves inflammation, and 10% or more improves fibrosis.
Physical activity: more than 150 minutes a week of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, tailored to the person. Normal-weight MASLD also benefits from diet and exercise.

Diet: calorie deficit built on unprocessed foods (vegetables, fruit, legumes, nuts, olive oil, fish, poultry); limit sugar-sweetened drinks and ultra-processed food. Coffee is associated with less liver damage.
Discourage alcohol in all; complete and permanent abstinence in significant (F2 or more) or advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis.
Bariatric surgery should be considered for eligible patients without cirrhosis; in compensated cirrhosis only after expert multidisciplinary review; it is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis.

sections.title: Drug therapy
items: Non-cirrhotic MASH with significant fibrosis (F2 to F3): consider resmetirom (EASL 2024, where approved). Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly also received US FDA approval in August 2025 for this group.
Treat comorbidities with drugs that also help the liver: GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, tirzepatide) for type 2 diabetes or obesity; they are safe in compensated cirrhosis.
Pioglitazone improves steatohepatitis in type 2 diabetes (AASLD 2023); EASL considers it safe but not a MASH-targeted therapy.

Vitamin E 800 IU daily may be considered in selected non-diabetic adults with biopsy-proven MASH (AASLD 2023); EASL 2024 does not recommend it because of limited evidence and long-term safety concerns.
Statins are safe and recommended for cardiovascular risk, including in compensated cirrhosis. SGLT2 inhibitors and metformin are safe for their usual indications but are not liver treatments.
Metformin, UDCA, silymarin and other nutraceuticals have no proven histological benefit and should not be used for the liver.

sections.title: Refer to hepatology
items: Intermediate or high risk on elastography or ELF, FIB-4 above 2.67, or discordant non-invasive tests.
Suspected cirrhosis (clinical signs, imaging, ELF above 11.3, or high liver stiffness), persistently raised ALT or AST, or diagnostic uncertainty.
Candidates for MASH-targeted drug therapy (F2 to F3) and patients considering bariatric surgery with advanced fibrosis.

sections.title: Follow-up and cirrhosis
items: Low risk: repeat FIB-4 every 1 to 3 years. Intermediate or high risk (F2 to F3): reassess annually with non-invasive tests.
Cirrhosis: ultrasound (with or without AFP) every 6 months for HCC; consider in F3 on individual risk. Not recommended below F3.

Liver stiffness 15 kPa or less with platelets 150 x 10^9/L or more makes clinically significant portal hypertension unlikely; stiffness 20 kPa or more or platelets below 150 x 10^9/L needs variceal screening unless already on a non-selective beta-blocker.

In cirrhosis: GLP-1 RA only in Child-Pugh A, SGLT2 inhibitors in Child-Pugh A and B, avoid metformin in decompensated cirrhosis and sulfonylureas in hepatic decompensation. Ensure high protein intake (1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day) to prevent sarcopenia.

sections.title: Special considerations
items: Use Asian BMI cut-offs: overweight 23 to 24.9 and obesity 25 kg/m2 or more. MASLD at normal BMI (lean MASLD) is common in South Asians and still needs fibrosis staging.
India: resmetirom and semaglutide 2.4 mg availability and approval status vary; lifestyle-based weight loss remains the core therapy.
Advanced MASH fibrosis: counsel first-degree relatives about their increased risk and offer them MASLD assessment (AASLD 2023).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Reassuring patients because ALT is normal: advanced fibrosis often has normal enzymes.
Skipping the alcohol history, and missing MetALD or alcohol-related disease.
Stopping or withholding statins because of fatty liver.
Using ultrasound grade of steatosis as a measure of severity instead of fibrosis staging.

drugs.name: Resmetirom
drugs.dose: 80 mg orally once daily if under 100 kg; 100 mg once daily if 100 kg or more
drugs.notes: Non-cirrhotic MASH with F2 to F3 fibrosis, with lifestyle therapy. Avoid with gemfibrozil (strong CYP2C8 inhibitor); limit statin doses per label; monitor liver tests and for gallbladder events.

drugs.name: Semaglutide (subcutaneous)
drugs.dose: Start 0.25 mg once weekly, increase every 4 weeks to a maintenance dose of 2.4 mg once weekly
drugs.notes: Obesity or non-cirrhotic MASH with F2 to F3 fibrosis; for type 2 diabetes use diabetes dosing. Nausea and vomiting common during titration.

drugs.name: Pioglitazone
drugs.dose: 30 mg orally once daily (range 15 to 45 mg)
drugs.notes: Type 2 diabetes with MASH; weight gain and fluid retention, avoid in heart failure.

drugs.name: Vitamin E (RRR-alpha-tocopherol)
drugs.notes: Selected non-diabetic adults with biopsy-proven MASH (AASLD); not recommended by EASL.
